title: Principal component analysis
summary: Centre the points, form the sample covariance with divisor n minus 1, and take its eigenvectors from the largest eigenvalue down. The variance fraction is that eigenvalue over the sum of the eigenvalues. The sign of an axis is arbitrary, mixed units should be standardised, and class labels are not used.
intuition:
Principal component analysis replaces a cloud of points by a new set of orthogonal coordinates ordered by how much variance they carry. The first step is to centre every column, so the sample mean of each feature is zero. The matrix that is diagonalised is the sample covariance $S$, with divisor $n-1$:
$$S_{jk}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_{ij} x_{ik}$$
once the columns are centred. The eigenvectors of $S$ are the principal axes. The largest eigenvalue comes first. Because $S$ is symmetric, those axes can be taken orthonormal, so the new coordinates are uncorrelated and geometrically perpendicular. The fraction of variance on axis $j$ is $\lambda_j$ divided by the sum of all the eigenvalues. Flipping the sign of an eigenvector does not change the axis or the fraction: $Sv=\lambda v$ implies $S(-v)=\lambda(-v)$.

Units matter before any of that linear algebra. If one feature is a large-unit copy of a small-unit feature, or simply has a much larger sample variance, it dominates $S$. The four-point example with coordinates $\pm 1$ and $\pm 10$, arranged so the sample covariance is diagonal, puts fraction $100/101$ of the variance on the large coordinate. Dividing each centred column by its sample standard deviation replaces $S$ by the correlation matrix and removes that accident of units. Standardise when the units differ. Leave the raw covariance alone only when the coordinates are already on a comparable scale.

Labels are not an input. The first principal axis maximises variance, not the gap between class means. A direction that separates classes and varies little will not be selected. The singular-value connection is the same spectral fact, read off the centred data matrix. If each row of the centred matrix $X$ is one point, the principal axes are the right singular vectors of $X$, and the eigenvalue of $S$ is the square of the corresponding singular value divided by $n-1$.

definitions.body: Each column has its sample mean subtracted. PCA diagonalises the covariance of these centred columns. Forgetting to centre folds the mean into the first direction.

The matrix $S$ with divisor $n-1$. This lesson uses that divisor, not $n$. The eigenvectors do not change if every entry of $S$ is multiplied by the same positive constant; the eigenvalues do. The variance fractions do not, because the constant cancels.
An eigenvector of $S$. Order them by decreasing eigenvalue. The fraction on component $j$ is $\lambda_j/\sum_i\lambda_i$. The sign of the vector is arbitrary.

If $X$ is the centred data matrix with one row per point and $X=U\Sigma V^\top$, the columns of $V$ are eigenvectors of $X^\top X$ and of $S=X^\top X/(n-1)$. They are the principal axes in the variable space. The matching eigenvalue is $\sigma_j^2/(n-1)$.

formulas.name: Sample covariance and the axis
formulas.note: $X$ is centred, with one row per point. $S$ uses divisor $n-1$. The largest $\lambda$ is the first principal component. Labels are not used.

formulas.name: Variance fraction
formulas.note: The same fraction is obtained if $S$ is replaced by $X^\top X$, because the divisor $n-1$ scales every eigenvalue equally. The sign of $v$ is arbitrary.

formulas.name: Singular values
formulas.note: Columns of $V$ are the right singular vectors of the centred matrix and the principal axes. Standardise columns before forming $S$ when the units differ, or a large-unit feature dominates.

properties: Centre first. On $(2,0)$, $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(0,-1)$ the means are already zero, the sample covariance is diagonal with entries $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$, and the first axis is along $(1,0)$ or $(-1,0)$.

The variance fraction is $\lambda_j$ over the sum of the eigenvalues. Here $(\tfrac83)/(\tfrac83+\tfrac23)=\tfrac45$, which is $80$ percent. Using divisor $n$ instead of $n-1$ scales both eigenvalues by $\tfrac34$ and leaves the fraction $\tfrac45$ unchanged.
The sign of a component is arbitrary. $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ are the same axis. The fraction does not depend on the sign.
Axes of a symmetric $S$ can be chosen orthogonal. In the diagonal example the coordinate axes are already orthogonal, and the off-diagonal entry of $S$ is $0$.

Standardise when units differ. On $(\pm 1,\pm 10)$ with all four sign patterns, the sample variances are $\tfrac43$ and $\tfrac{400}{3}$, the covariance is $0$, and the leading fraction is $\tfrac{100}{101}$. After dividing each centred column by its sample standard deviation, each variance is $1$ and neither axis dominates by units.
PCA does not maximise class separation. It never reads a label. A direction that separates classes can be a small-eigenvalue direction and be discarded.

examples.title: Four centred points, a diagonal covariance
examples.prompt: Points $(2,0)$, $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(0,-1)$. Use the sample covariance with divisor $n-1$. Find the first principal axis and its variance fraction. Check the singular-value relation.
steps: The coordinate means are both $0$, so the points are already centred. Sum of squares of the first coordinate is $4+4+0+0=8$, so $S_{11}=8/3$. Sum of squares of the second is $0+0+1+1=2$, so $S_{22}=2/3$. The cross sum is $0$, so $S_{12}=0$.

The eigenvalues are $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$, with eigenvectors along $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The larger one comes first, so the first principal axis is the first coordinate axis. The opposite vector $(-1,0)$ is the same axis.

The variance fraction is $(\tfrac83)/(\tfrac{10}{3})=\tfrac45$. As a singular-value check: $X^\top X=\mathrm{diag}(8,2)$, singular values $\sqrt{8}$ and $\sqrt{2}$, and $\sigma^2/(n-1)$ recovers $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$.
examples.answer: The first principal axis is along $(1,0)$, sign arbitrary, and the variance fraction is $\tfrac45$.

examples.title: A large unit takes the first axis
examples.prompt: Points $(1,10)$, $(1,-10)$, $(-1,10)$, and $(-1,-10)$, sample covariance with divisor $n-1$. What fraction of variance lies on the second coordinate, and what happens if each centred column is divided by its sample standard deviation?
steps: Both means are $0$. Sum of squares of the first coordinate is $4$, so its sample variance is $\tfrac43$. Sum of squares of the second is $400$, so its sample variance is $\tfrac{400}{3}$. The cross term $10-10-10+10=0$, so the covariance is diagonal.
The leading eigenvalue is $\tfrac{400}{3}$. The fraction is $400/(400+4)=\tfrac{100}{101}$. The first principal axis is the second coordinate, the large-unit one, or its opposite sign.

The sample standard deviations are $\sqrt{4/3}$ and $10\sqrt{4/3}$. Dividing each centred column by its own sample standard deviation makes both sample variances equal to $1$ and keeps the covariance $0$. Each eigenvalue is then $1$, and the fraction on each axis is $\tfrac12$. The unit no longer chooses the axis.
examples.answer: Before standardising, the large coordinate carries fraction $\tfrac{100}{101}$. After standardising, the fraction on each axis is $\tfrac12$.

traps: Forgetting to centre. The matrix $X^\top X/(n-1)$ is the sample covariance only after each column has mean zero. A nonzero mean leaks into that product.

Thinking the variance fraction changes when the divisor changes from $n-1$ to $n$. Both eigenvalues scale by the same constant, so $(\tfrac83)/(\tfrac{10}{3})$ stays $\tfrac45$. The eigenvectors stay put. The lesson still reports the $n-1$ eigenvalues $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$, not the unscaled sums of squares.
Treating $(1,0)$ and $(-1,0)$ as different components. The sign of a principal axis is arbitrary. Both vectors span the first coordinate axis of the four-point example.

Skipping standardisation when units differ. Variances $\tfrac43$ and $\tfrac{400}{3}$ put fraction $\tfrac{100}{101}$ on the large coordinate even though the two coordinates were built as matching sign patterns.

Choosing the first principal component to maximise the distance between class means. PCA does not use labels. Class separation is the job of LDA, which shares one covariance and has a linear boundary.
Calling the left singular vectors the axes in variable space. With one row per point, the principal axes are the right singular vectors, the columns of $V$ in $X=U\Sigma V^\top$.
python:
# Centred points (2,0), (-2,0), (0,1), (0,-1). Divisor n-1 = 3.
pts = [(2, 0), (-2, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]
n = 4
assert abs(sum(p[0] for p in pts) / n) < 1e-12
assert abs(sum(p[1] for p in pts) / n) < 1e-12
sxx = sum(p[0] ** 2 for p in pts) / (n - 1)
syy = sum(p[1] ** 2 for p in pts) / (n - 1)
sxy = sum(p[0] * p[1] for p in pts) / (n - 1)
assert abs(sxx - 8 / 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(syy - 2 / 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(sxy) < 1e-12
fraction = sxx / (sxx + syy)
assert abs(fraction - 0.8) < 1e-12
# Right-singular-value check: sigma^2 / (n-1) recovers the eigenvalues.
assert abs((8 / (n - 1)) - sxx) < 1e-12
# Large-unit fraction 100/101 on the second coordinate.
big = (400 / 3) / (400 / 3 + 4 / 3)
assert abs(big - 100 / 101) < 1e-12
print(round(100 * fraction))

questions.stem: The centred points are $(2,0)$, $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(0,-1)$. The sample covariance uses divisor $n-1$. The first principal axis is
options: the zero vector, because the points are centred
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

The sample variances are $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$, and the covariance is $0$. The larger eigenvalue belongs to the first coordinate. Centring makes the mean zero; it does not make the leading eigenvector zero. The sign of that eigenvector is arbitrary, so $(-1,0)$ is the same axis.

questions.stem: Points $(1,10)$, $(1,-10)$, $(-1,10)$, and $(-1,-10)$ use the sample covariance with divisor $n-1$. The fraction of variance on the second coordinate is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $\tfrac{100}{101}$.

Both means are $0$ and the cross term is $0$. Sample variances are $\tfrac43$ and $\tfrac{400}{3}$. The second eigenvalue over the sum is $400/(400+4)=\tfrac{100}{101}$. The fraction $\tfrac12$ is what remains after each column is standardised. The fraction $\tfrac45$ belongs to the other worked example.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true of PCA as used in this lesson?
options: The columns are centred before the covariance is formed.
The covariance $S$ uses the sample divisor $n-1$.
The sign of a principal-axis vector is arbitrary.
The first principal component is chosen to maximise the distance between class means.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

Centring makes $S=X^\top X/(n-1)$ the sample covariance, and $Sv=\lambda v$ is unchanged when $v$ is replaced by $-v$. Class means are never read. Maximising the gap between class means is a supervised goal, the LDA goal, not PCA.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: Eigenvectors of the symmetric sample covariance can be taken to be orthogonal.
When units differ, standardise, or the large-unit feature can dominate the covariance.
With one row per centred point, the principal axes are the right singular vectors of that matrix.
Replacing the divisor $n-1$ by $n$ changes the variance fraction $\lambda_j/\sum_i\lambda_i$.
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

A real symmetric matrix has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. The $(\pm 1,\pm 10)$ example puts fraction $\tfrac{100}{101}$ on the large coordinate until the columns are scaled by their sample standard deviations. The right singular vectors of the centred matrix diagonalise $X^\top X$ and therefore $S$. D is false: a common scale factor cancels in the fraction, even though it changes the eigenvalues themselves.

questions.stem: The centred points are $(2,0)$, $(-2,0)$, $(0,1)$, and $(0,-1)$. The sample covariance uses divisor $n-1$. Enter the percentage of variance on the first principal component, as an integer.
questions.solution:
The answer is **80**.

The eigenvalues are $\tfrac83$ and $\tfrac23$. The leading fraction is $(\tfrac83)/(\tfrac{10}{3})=\tfrac45=0.80$, so the integer percentage is $80$.
